During this lab we will attempt to replicate some of the results in @dizon2019parents. The data you have been provided does not need much cleaning. However, you may will not get the exact same results as those shown in the paper because some variables are missing and there are small sample size differences. For the most part, your results should be very similar. 

# Context

This RCT was used as an example in [Lecture 6](lecture-6-multi.qmd). 

- **Setting:** primary schools in Machinga and Balaka districts, Malawi, in 2012. Primary school is technically free but still costly: parents spend about 1,750 MWK (US$10.6) per child per year. Schools must send report cards home each term, but 60% of parents say they don’t know their child’s performance from the last report, because the card never arrived or they couldn’t understand it.

- **Sample:** The sampling frame includes households with at least two children in grades 2–6, with two children randomly chosen per household. Of 3,451 sampled households, 2,634 were eligible and surveyed, giving 5,268 parent–child pairs.

- **Randomization:** households were randomly split half into treatment and half into control. Randomization was stratified on the between-sibling score gap and the estimated literacy rate in the household’s village, a proxy for parental education. Half of the treatment group also received more detailed skills information, but the paper pools all treated households and finds no separate effect.

- **Intervention:** surveyors visited every household and ran a baseline survey on spending and beliefs about each child’s scores. In the same visit, treatment parents were walked through an easy-to-read report card for each child, showing math, English, Chichewa and overall scores, grades and class rank.

- **Outcomes:** an endline survey immediately after the visit measured updated beliefs, the free workbook level chosen and willingness to pay for remedial textbooks. Longer-run outcomes came from school attendance records in the following month and a second endline survey about a year later, covering enrolment and spending, for a random subset of about 900 households.

# Setup

On Moodle, under "Week 8", you find the ["Lab 3 Data"](https://moody.st-andrews.ac.uk/moodle/mod/folder/view.php?id=1572527) folder.

1. Create a folder on OneDrive (or your H drive) for "Lab 3"

2. Download the paper, store it in this folder, and open it on your computer. You will need to reference the various tables and figures. 

3. Download the "dizonross2019.dta" file and store it in this folder. 

4. Open Stata and create a new .do file. Save it as "Lab 2/lab-2.do"

5. Add the following to your .do file; editing the file path to match your folder structure.

```{stata}
*| eval: false

* ============================================================================ *

* ============================================================================ *
```

```{stata}
*| include: false
use "$data_dir\dizonross2019.dta", clear
bys hhid (child): gen ave_12 = score_ave[1]-score_ave[2] 
```

## User-written packages

In this lab you will make tables of summary statistics and regression output; just as you see in the paper. This is an important skill needed for the project. Most researchers use user-written packages like `outreg2` and `estout` to do this. Unfortunately, these cannot be installed in the AppsAnywhere version of Stata, so we will make use of Stata's `dtable` and `etable` commands. They get the job done, but are not as user-friendly. If you have access to your own Stata license, consider investigating these other options. 

There is also a popular regression model package called `reghdfe` which is used to estimate models with fixed effects. We will use an alternative called `areg`. 

:::{.callout-note title="Installing packages"}
Many user-written packages can be installed as follows: `ssc install reghdfe`.
:::

# Replication

## Assignment

We begin by understanding assignment and validating randomization. The main variable of interest is the dummy variable `treat`, which =1 for the treated households. 

1. Use the command `codebook` to figure out how many unique schools. 

2. Use the command below to figure out if there are 

```{stata}
*| eval: false

duplicates report hhid
```

3. Create a frequency table of the treatment indicator `treat`. Is this an efficient experiment design?

Next, we will try to replicate some of the lines in Table 1 (the balance table). 
`
4. We will begin by replicating some of the lines under "Panel A. Respondent background." These are background characteristics of the parent who responded to the survey. 

   - In the main Stata window, go to "Statistics > Summaries, tables, and tests > Table of descriptive statistics". 
   - Under "Variables (optional):" list `resp_female` `resp_decides` `resp_age` `resp_secondary`.
   - Select "Describe variables by group"
   - Under "Variable that defines groups:" select `treat`
   - Change "Tests across groups:" to "Show"
   - Submit
   
   Your results should replicate:
   
```{stata}
*| echo: false

dtable resp_female resp_decides resp_age resp_secondary, by(treat, tests)
```   

:::{.callout-caution title="Unequal variance"}
This test assumes equal variance across treatment and control. The reported $p$-value comes from a simple regression of the variable on a treatment dummy. This is not necessarily a significant deal, since baseline covariates should not be an outcome of the experiment.  
:::

5. Follow the same steps replicating lines from "Panel C. Student information" for variables `grade`, `child_age`, `child_female`, and `attend_bl`.

6. Does the evidence support the researchers claim that assignment into treatment is balanced (p. 2744)?

:::{.callout-warning}
**Don't forget to store a copy of your code in the .do file.**
:::

## Graphical analysis

In this section we are going to attempt to replicate Figure 3.

1. Replicate Panel A. 
  
   - In the main Stata window, go to "Graphics > Bar chart"
   - Under "Statistics to plot" select `belief_err_bl`
   - Under the "Categories" tab, select "Group 1" and find the variable `treat`
   - Under the "Bars" tab, under "Bar labels", select "Label with bar height"
   - Submit
   
   Your results should replicate:
   
```{stata}
*| echo: false

graph bar (mean) belief_err_bl, over(treat) blabel(bar)
```   
   
2. Replicate Panel C. Follow the same steps as above, but use `belief_err_end` instead. 

3. To replicate Panel B, you will need to use the `twoway` graph function. We have used this in previous labs. We won't try to estimate the flexible functions shown in the paper. Instead, we will use the `lfit` option to fit a linear line between `belief_bl` and `score_ave` for both the treated and control groups. Here is my version. 

```{stata}
*| echo: false

twoway (lfit belief_bl score_ave if treat==0, lc(blue))  (lfit belief_bl score_ave if treat==1, lp(dash) lc(green)) (function y = x, range(0 100) lc(gs8)), ylabel(0(20)100) xlabel(0(20)100) legend(order(1 "Control" 2 "Treat") ring(0) pos(5))
```  

4. Replicate Panel D using similar steps. The lines should have a similar slope. 

:::{.callout-warning}
**Don't forget to store a copy of your code in the .do file.**
:::


## ATE

One of the main outcomes in the study is `belief_end`: which captures the parents' beliefs about their children's performances **after** the intervention. 

1. Test whether there is a statistically significant difference between the mean of `belief_end` across treatment groups. To do so, we will first use Stata's `ttest` command. 

   - In the main Stata window, go to "Statistics > Summaries, tables, and tests > Classical tests of hypotheses > t-test (mean-comparison test)"
   - Select "Two-sample using groups"
   - Under "Variable name:" select `belief_end`
   - Under "Group variable name" select `treat`
   - Submit
   
   Your results should replicate:

```{stata}
*| echo: false

ttest belief_end, by(treat)
```      
   
2. Now, go through the same steps but select option "unequal variances". This should compute the Neyman variance estimator. 

3. Replicate these results by estimating a linear regression. The default estimated SE should replicate that from Q1.

4. Estimate the same simple regression using option `vce(robust)` (HC1) and `vce(hc2)`. These two should be very similar, since treatment is close to 50-50. 

## Regression adjustment

Now we can replicate some of the regression tables. 

1. The variables `wb_math` and `wb_engl` take on values $\{-1,0,1\}$. Recode these values to $\{0,100,200\}$. You can either use `recode` or `replace`. 

```{stata}
*| eval: false

recode wb_math (-1 = 0) (0 = 100) (1 = 200)
** or
* replace wb_math = (wb_math+1)*100
```  

```{stata}
*| echo: false
recode wb_math (-1 = 0) (0 = 100) (1 = 200)
recode wb_engl (-1 = 0) (0 = 100) (1 = 200)
```

2. Estimate the first model from Panel A. of Table A.1 (p. 2759), including the following controls and estimating robust SEs

```{stata}
reg belief_end treat par_educ resp_female resp_literate ave_12 score_ave child_female i.grade , vce(robust)
``` 

3. Next we will try to estimate the remaining models and create a table. 

   - Estimate each model and store the results as follows. You can add the option `quietly` to stop Stata printing the results of each model.

```{stata}
*| eval: false
qui reg belief_end treat par_educ resp_female resp_literate ave_12 score_ave child_female i.grade , vce(robust)
  est store model1
``` 

   - For each additional model, you need to change the name of the stored results: `model1`, `model2`, etc.
   
   - Use the following code to make a table:
   
```{stata}
*| eval: false
etable, est(model1 model2 model3 model4 model5 model6 model7) column(depvar) keep(treat) eqrecode(belief_end = xb wb_math = xb wb_engl = xb lnwtp_math_engl = xb enrolled = xb ln_educ_exp_end = xb attend_admin = xb) novarlabel cstat(_r_b, nformat(%5.4f)) cstat(_r_se, nformat(%5.4f)) showstars showstarsnote stars(.1 "*" .05 "**" .01 "***") mstat(N) mstat(r2, nformat(%4.3f))
  
  // the code adjusts the default star symbols to match Econ standard
  // the code only displays the coefficient on treat
  // the code uses eqrecode() to make coefficients from different equations present side-by-side
```

The following information is provided in the tables notes of Table A.1

> "Standard errors are clustered at the household level. Regressions control for school FE, average parental years of education, parent gender, a parental education proxy used for stratification, the between-child score gap, child baseline performance, child gender, grade FE, and the baseline value of the dependent variable (baseline value not available for enrollment or experimental outcomes)."

4. Evidently, the model specifications in Q.3 do not perfectly match those in the paper. We are missing school fixed effects (FE), have replaced "a parental education proxy used for stratification" with `resp_literate`. When there is a large number of FEs (as here), it makes sense to use a slightly different estimator. Run the following code to `absorb` the FEs using the command `areg`. Does it make a difference to either the estimated coefficient or SE?

```{stata}
*| eval: false
areg belief_end treat par_educ resp_female resp_literate ave_12 score_ave child_female i.grade , absorb(school) vce(robust)
``` 

5. The authors do not estimate heteroskedastic-robust SEs. Instead, the estimate SEs that are cluster-robust, where the cluster variable is the household. This is because there are two children in the data for every household. We can do this as follows. 

```{stata}
*| eval: false
areg belief_end treat par_educ resp_female resp_literate ave_12 score_ave child_female i.grade , absorb(school) vce(cluster hhid)
``` 

6. Create the following table and comment on whether the various regression adjustments and SE estimates have a big impact on the estimated ATE. 

```{stata}
*| eval: false
est clear
qui reg belief_end treat, vce(robust) 
	est store model1
	
qui reg belief_end treat par_educ resp_female resp_literate ave_12 score_ave child_female i.grade, vce(robust)
	est store model2

qui areg belief_end treat par_educ resp_female resp_literate ave_12 score_ave child_female i.grade, absorb(school) vce(robust)
	est store model3
	
qui areg belief_end treat par_educ resp_female resp_literate ave_12 score_ave child_female i.grade, absorb(school) vce(cluster hhid)
	est store model4

	
etable, est(model1 model2 model3 model4) keep(treat) column(estimates) novarlabel cstat(_r_b, nformat(%5.4f)) cstat(_r_se, nformat(%5.4f)) showstars showstarsnote stars(.1 "*" .05 "**" .01 "***")
```


## Interacted model

In the paper, the authors focus on a model that interacts the treatment with baseline academic achievement (see p. 2747). The results are shown in Table 2. 

$$
  y_{ij} = c_o + c_1A_{ij}\times Treat_i + c_2A_{ij} + c_3Treat_i + c_4'X_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij}
$$

1. Here is an example of how to estimate this model for the outcome `belief_end`. Here I am excluding the FEs and estimating heteroskedastic-robust SEs.

```{stata}
*| eval: false

reg belief_end i.treat##c.score_ave par_educ resp_literate ave_12 child_female i.grade resp_female, vce(robust)
  // since score_ave is a continous variable you must use notation c.
```

2. Create a table that replicates the results of columns (1)-(4) in Table 2. As above, you can exclude school FEs and estimate heteroskedastic-robust SEs. Try to replicate the following output. 

```{stata}
*| echo: false

est clear

qui reg belief_end i.treat##c.score_ave par_educ resp_literate  ave_12 child_female i.grade resp_female, vce(cluster hhid)
	est store model1
	
qui reg wb_math i.treat##c.score_ave par_educ resp_literate  ave_12 child_female i.grade resp_female, vce(cluster hhid)
	est store model2
	
qui reg wb_engl i.treat##c.score_ave par_educ resp_literate  ave_12 child_female i.grade resp_female, vce(cluster hhid)
	est store model3
	
qui reg lnwtp_math_engl i.treat##c.score_ave par_educ resp_literate  ave_12 child_female i.grade resp_female, vce(cluster hhid)
	est store model4	
	
etable, est(model1 model2 model3 model4) column(depvar) keep(1.treat 1.treat#c.score_ave score_ave) eqrecode(belief_end = xb wb_math = xb wb_engl = xb lnwtp_math_engl = xb) novarlabel cstat(_r_b, nformat(%5.4f)) cstat(_r_se, nformat(%5.4f)) showstars showstarsnote stars(.1 "*" .05 "**" .01 "***") mstat(N) mstat(r2, nformat(%4.3f))
```

3. Now try to replicate *Panel A. Continuous versions* from Table 3 (which focuses on non-experimental outcomes).

```{stata}
*| echo: false

est clear
  
qui reg enrolled i.treat##c.score_ave par_educ resp_literate  ave_12 child_female i.grade resp_female, vce(robust)
	est store model1
	
qui reg ln_educ_exp_end i.treat##c.score_ave par_educ resp_literate  ave_12 child_female i.grade resp_female, vce(robust)
	est store model2
	
qui reg attend_admin i.treat##c.score_ave par_educ resp_literate  ave_12 child_female i.grade resp_female, vce(robust)
	est store model3
	
etable, est(model1 model2 model3) column(depvar) keep(1.treat 1.treat#c.score_ave score_ave) eqrecode(enrolled = xb ln_educ_exp_end = xb attend_admin = xb) novarlabel cstat(_r_b, nformat(%5.4f)) cstat(_r_se, nformat(%5.4f)) showstars showstarsnote stars(.1 "*" .05 "**" .01 "***") mstat(N) mstat(r2, nformat(%4.3f))

```

4. To replicate *Panel B. Binary versions* you first need to create a variable that is a dummy variable called `above_median`: =1 if `score_ave` is above the sample median and =0 otherwise. Try to do this, and then estimate a model that interacts `treat` with `above_median`: `i.treat##i.above_median` (since both are discrete). Your results should look like. 

```{stata}
*| echo: false

qui sum score_ave, det
qui gen above_median = score_ave>r(p50) if !missing(score_ave)

est clear
  
qui reg enrolled i.treat##i.above_median par_educ resp_literate  ave_12 child_female i.grade resp_female, vce(robust)
	est store model1
	
qui reg ln_educ_exp_end i.treat##i.above_median par_educ resp_literate  ave_12 child_female i.grade resp_female, vce(robust)
	est store model2
	
qui reg attend_admin i.treat##i.above_median par_educ resp_literate  ave_12 child_female i.grade resp_female, vce(robust)
	est store model3
	
etable, est(model1 model2 model3) column(depvar) keep(1.treat 1.treat#1.above_median 1.above_median) eqrecode(enrolled = xb ln_educ_exp_end = xb attend_admin = xb) novarlabel cstat(_r_b, nformat(%5.4f)) cstat(_r_se, nformat(%5.4f)) showstars showstarsnote stars(.1 "*" .05 "**" .01 "***") mstat(N) mstat(r2, nformat(%4.3f))
```

## Heterogeneity

Heterogeneity is a crucial step in any paper where the researcher tests to see whether the treatment effect varies with certain characteristics of the sample. Here, the author focuses on parental education. 

1. As a final exercise try to replicate the results shown in *Panel B. Heterogeneity in the treatment effect on the slope, by parent education, for selected experimental outcomes* of Table 4. 

::: {.callout-note title="Interactions"}
A triple interaction, `i.treat ##c.score_ave##c.par_educ`, includes all three variables, all three two-way interactions, and the three-way interaction. For the workbook outcomes, use the subject-specific scores `score_math` and `score_engl` instead of `score_ave`.
:::

## Replicate

1. Check that all the code you executed is in the .do file. 

2. Make sure your .do file is saved. 

3. Run the whole .do file to check that the results replicate.
